title: How Will the Midterms Shape the Rest of Trump's Presidency?
question: How will the 2026 midterm results shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency?
description: Democrats won both houses of the US Congress in the 3 November 2026 midterms. Here is what that means for vetoes, budgets, judges, investigations and executive orders over Donald Trump's final two years, with the arguments from both parties. Will divided government bring compromise or gridlock?

ad_safety.reason: A divisive political topic the day after an election; handled neutrally with both parties' views attributed, but it may still get limited ads.

sources.title: NPR: Democrats win full control of Congress, ushering in a new era of divided government
NBC News: Democrats win control of the House and vow to keep Trump in check
TIME: Democrats Win House and Senate, live election updates

PBS NewsHour live updates: a look at recent midterm results
US Constitution, Article I, Section 7 (veto override) and Article I, Sections 2-3 (impeachment)

scenes.narration: How will the midterms shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency? Overnight, American voters handed both houses of Congress to the opposition Democrats.

visual.text: How will the midterms shape Trump's last two years?

scenes.narration: By early Wednesday, The Associated Press tally gave Democrats the House and at least fifty-two Senate seats, plus two independents who usually vote with them.
So for the next two years, the president and the lawmakers who write the laws come from rival parties. Here is how that changes what Trump can and cannot do.

visual.text: What can a president do without Congress?

scenes.narration: Every two years, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of the 100 Senate seats are up for election.
Before the vote, Republicans held the Senate fifty-three to forty-seven. Democrats flipped seven seats, including Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and Maine.
In Texas, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton, making him the first Democrat to win a statewide race there in more than thirty years.

visual.label: Texas Senate flips
visual.sub: First statewide Democratic win in 30+ years

scenes.narration: In the House, NBC News projects Democrats will hold around 255 seats, well past the 218 needed for a majority. A few races are still being counted.
Midterms usually punish the president's party. In 2018, during Trump's first term, Democrats gained forty House seats. In 2006, under George W. Bush, they took both chambers.
Campaigns focused on the cost of living and on corruption claims, and Trump's approval rating went into election day below forty percent.
The new Congress is sworn in on 3 January 2027. From then on, nothing Trump wants can become law unless both chambers pass it.
It works the other way too. Democrats can pass bills, but the president can veto them, and overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers.

visual.label: Two-thirds needed to override a veto

scenes.narration: Democrats do not have anywhere near two-thirds. So most of their agenda, on health costs, tariffs and redistricting, is likely to stop at the president's desk.

visual.label: Veto
visual.sub: Bills stop at the president's desk

scenes.narration: Trump saw this coming. In a podcast interview the day before the vote, he said:

visual.text: So what did Trump say he would do?

scenes.narration: I'll become Mr. Veto, and then at some point we'll probably make deals.

visual.text: I'll become Mr. Veto, and then at some point we'll probably make deals.
visual.who: Donald Trump, Pod Force One, 2 Nov 2026

scenes.narration: That is the usual pattern of divided government: long standoffs, then narrow deals on the few things both sides need.
The biggest of those is money. Congress must pass twelve annual spending bills, or a deal covering them, to keep the federal government open.
The US budget year starts on 1 October. If no spending law is signed by then, parts of the government shut down.
With a Democratic Congress and a Republican president, both sides hold a veto over the other's priorities, so every deadline becomes a bargaining chip.
The national borrowing limit, the debt ceiling, was raised by five trillion dollars in July 2025, which may push that particular fight further down the road.
The Senate has a power the House does not: it confirms judges, Cabinet members and other top officials. It takes a simple majority.
With Democrats running the Senate, NPR reports, the steady confirmation of Trump-nominated judges is expected to slow sharply.
Federal judges serve for life, so every seat filled or left empty shapes American law for decades, long after this presidency ends.
Any new Cabinet nominee will now need at least a handful of Democratic votes to be confirmed.

visual.label: A handful of Democratic votes needed

scenes.narration: Control of the House means control of its committees, and committees can issue subpoenas: legal orders to hand over documents or testify.
Democrats say they will investigate the president's family business deals, cryptocurrency ventures, immigration enforcement and the independence of the Justice Department.
What about impeachment? The House can impeach with a simple majority, but removing a president needs a two-thirds vote in the Senate.
No president has ever been removed that way. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries says his party has not ruled impeachment in or out.
Republicans see the coming investigations differently. Senate Republican leader John Thune wrote early on Wednesday:

visual.label: The Republican view
visual.sub: Defend the record of the last two years

scenes.narration: Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we've done.

visual.text: Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we've done.
visual.who: John Thune, Senate Republican leader, 4 Nov 2026

scenes.narration: Blocked in Congress, presidents usually lean harder on executive orders: instructions to government agencies that do not need a vote.
Congress can cancel an order by passing a law, but the president can veto that law too. So the real check on executive orders is usually the courts.
Other democracies know this tension well. In France, a president facing a hostile parliament is called cohabitation, and it has happened three times since 1986.
For the rest of the world, the practical effect is that Washington's big new policies, on trade, aid or war, now need either a deal or a signature.

visual.label: Global effects of a split Washington

scenes.narration: Trump's second term ends on 20 January 2029, and the US Constitution bars him from a third. These two years become the opening act of 2028.
Democrats will try to show they can govern. Republicans will argue that a hostile Congress is blocking the president's agenda. Voters will judge both in 2028.
So: one election, and for the next two years the president needs his opponents for almost every new law, budget and nominee.
Here is the question for you. Will divided government force compromise, or just two years of gridlock? Tell us in the comments.
